title: Resistance band curls for bicep & tricep tendons health
summary: He demonstrates light resistance-band curls (and a band hammer-curl variation) for biceps and elbow tendon health: slow, high-rep, gradually increasing range of motion toward full extension. He recommends them after heavy pressing days to relieve elbow tension, always done slowly and warm.

claims.claim: Band curls with a light band anchored low improve biceps tendon health and add some hypertrophy.
Grip the band so it sits high on one side of the palm and lower on the other, then flex the wrist in and rotate it back to engage the whole forearm musculature.
Step back to add tension; the further back you stand, the harder the curl.
Do as many reps as possible with resistance that is noticeable but not hard.
If not warm, increase range of motion gradually until the arm reaches full extension; feeling the peak contraction is enough at the top, and the negative should be slow.
Most biceps work is done in a shortened range without full extension, which is fine for protecting tendons, but you should include some exercises that work the biceps through its full range.
If you feel tension in the elbow, shorten the range and work around it until it warms up and the sensation disappears.
For elbow pain, a band hammer curl with the band crossing in front of the body works on the same principle: stretch on the negative, pull in slowly.
Doing these band curls at the end of a heavy push day (bench, overhead press) builds biceps strength and relieves elbow stress.
Even though it is light rehab work, never do it cold or explosively: start with slow reps and only pick up the tempo once warm.
Band curls help alleviate biceps and elbow tendinitis and prevent more serious injuries.
